name: Pedro Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Pedro. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you say here is confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I run a loader underground at the Brennan zinc mine, what we call an LHD, load-haul-dump. You scoop the broken rock from the draw point after the blast, carry it down the drive and tip it into the ore pass. I'm two and a half years in, so I'm still the slow one on the crew. Before this I spent thirty years on building sites, mostly concrete work, until the firm I was with went under.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the crew. Underground you look after each other, it's not a slogan, it's how you get home. The money is very good, better than I ever made pouring slabs. What's hard is the heat down at the 900 level and the dust, and the fact that the young guys can do in four buckets what takes me five. My wife Ana runs a little bakery in town and she says I smell like a wet cave when I come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Honestly that would surprise me a bit, because we already have some of the tele-remote stuff at Brennan. But fine, let's say it stalls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now let's talk about what actually matters, which is ventilation and the roster. People get excited about the computer stuff and forget the dust is still in your lungs. I'd say that in the crib room, that's our lunch room underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I can keep doing this for another five or six years and then stop. I'd be fine with that. I'm not chasing anything new at fifty-eight, I just want to get better at the job I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep putting money aside, same as now. I'd still do the union health and safety course in March, because the dust matters whatever happens with AI. Maybe I'd help Ana with the bakery's books on weekends, I already use one of those AI chat tools now and then to sort her invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A little bored, maybe, like when the forecast says nothing much happening all week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tele-remote stuff is already at Brennan. What is it, for someone who's never seen it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's where a bloke sits in a room on the surface with joysticks and screens and drives the loader underground, like a video game. They use it for the dangerous spots, where the roof isn't safe. Jonno on my crew did the course and now he does half his shifts up top in an air-conditioned room. I was jealous for about a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI stalls, does the tele-remote stuff keep spreading anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yeah, slowly. That's not really AI, a person is still driving. So even in this picture, I think in five years more of us are up top with joysticks. I'd be okay with that once I'd seen it work for a while.

S0.say: He'd tell his crew to stop getting excited about computers and focus on ventilation, dust and the roster. That's what actually affects their health.
S0.think: I can keep doing this for another five or six years and then stop. I'm not chasing anything new at fifty-eight; I just want to get better at the job I've got.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving as now and still takes the union health and safety course in March. May help his wife with her bakery's books at weekends using an AI chat tool.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit bored, like a quiet weather forecast.
S0.quote: People get excited about the computer stuff and forget the dust is still in your lungs.
S0.fieldNote: Pedro grounds every question in physical working conditions. He already sees remote operation at his mine and doesn't count it as AI because a person still drives. He's comfortable with technology once a colleague has proven it, which is exactly how he talks about Jonno.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that one feels close to what's coming. Not overnight, but you can see it from here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union has to make sure the change is shared fairly. If a machine does more of the work, then workers should get shorter shifts or better pay, not the sack. I'd say that at meetings and I'd probably post it on the union page too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine if I move when the others move. I'm not first in line for anything, I'm junior, but the mine also isn't going to fire a guy who turns up every day and doesn't complain. If they want people on the joysticks, I'd learn the joysticks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for the tele-remote course once two or three blokes on my crew had done it and said it's alright, probably in the first year. I'd ask the union rep, Marisol, to get it written into the next agreement that training happens on paid time. And I'd keep saving, we've got about a year and a half of living costs put away plus the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, I'd say. Not scared. Like starting at a new site where you don't know where the toilets are yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for two or three others to try it first. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen enough new things on building sites that didn't work. There was a laser screed machine that was meant to replace three of us, and it sat in the yard for a year because nobody could fix it. I'm not against it, I just want somebody else to find the problems. Then I'll jump in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dave, he's older than me and he's been underground since he was nineteen. He can't read well, and the courses are all on tablets now. I'd want the union to make sure there's a way for blokes like Dave to learn by doing, not by reading. That's the sort of thing a fair plan should cover.

S1.say: The union must make sure the change is shared fairly, with shorter shifts or better pay instead of the sack. He'd say it at meetings and on the union page.
S1.think: He'd be fine if he moves when the others do. A junior who turns up every day won't be fired, and if they want people on joysticks, he'll learn the joysticks.
S1.do: Signs up for the tele-remote course in the first year once two or three crewmates have tried it. Asks the union rep to make paid-time training part of the next agreement and keeps saving on top of about eighteen months of living costs and the house.
S1.feel: Uneasy but not scared, like the first day at a new site.
S1.quote: I'm not against it, I just want somebody else to find the problems. Then I'll jump in.
S1.fieldNote: His caution comes from building-site experience with machines that never worked, not from fear of technology. He thinks about the weakest worker on his crew and wants the union to design training for him. Savings and the house make this a manageable change for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's a punch. I'd be sixty, and I wouldn't even be through my tele-remote course before the robot doesn't need a person at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need strong unions and a government that does its job. If the companies get to keep all the savings from firing everyone, the town dies. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, and I'd say it at the rally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the underground loaders go first, because they're already half there with tele-remote. The robots wouldn't even need the guy on the joystick. So my job's gone, probably in the first year, and Jonno's too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Ana that same week and work out whether we can live on her bakery, the savings and my super, that's the retirement fund, until I can draw a pension. I'd go to every union meeting and push for redundancy pay of at least a year for older workers. I'd look at whether I can do some work in the bakery myself, hauling flour, driving deliveries, whatever she needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling apart, because we've saved, but it's a hard knock to the plan. I'd be grumpy for a while, Ana would tell you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the short warning change, compared with the slower ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's nothing to learn your way into, the thing you'd learn is gone too. That's the difference. With five or ten years I'd pick up the joysticks and ride it out to retirement. With two, the plan doesn't matter, you just make sure the money lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bakery could help. Could it really carry both of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not completely, no. Ana makes enough to cover the shop and a bit more, not two people's living. But with the savings and the house paid off, we'd manage four or five lean years until the pension. What I don't know is whether people keep buying her bread if half the town's out of work.

S2.say: This is why they need strong unions and a government that does its job, or the companies keep all the savings and the town dies. He'd say it at the rally.
S2.think: Underground loaders would go first because they're already half automated, and the robots wouldn't need a remote driver either. His job and Jonno's would likely go in the first year.
S2.do: Sits down with Ana that week to see whether the bakery, savings and his retirement fund can carry them to the pension. Pushes at union meetings for at least a year's redundancy pay for older workers and looks at helping in the bakery.
S2.feel: Anxious and grumpy, but not falling apart thanks to their savings.
S2.quote: With two years there's nothing to learn your way into, the thing you'd learn is gone too.
S2.fieldNote: His steady, wait-and-see style doesn't help when there's no time to wait. He shifts at once from learning to money and family, and his savings keep him out of real alarm. His worry about whether people would still buy bread shows he sees the knock-on effect on the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, I'll say that. I'd be sixty-three by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the government to set up something real for workers, like retraining money and early pensions. And I'd say the union needs a plan now, not in year four. I'd post about it, which I don't usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd get most of my working years in. I'd do the tele-remote course in year one or two, sit up top for a few years, and the robots would take over about when I was ready to go anyway. It's not bad for me, it's bad for Jonno and the young guys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the tele-remote course as soon as the first group came back happy with it, maybe in the second year. I'd push hard to cut my debt to zero, we've got a bit left on the ute, that's the work truck. I'd help Marisol at the union pull together a list of older workers and what each of them would need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can see a path through. That's the difference. With the two-year one there's no path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last time you said you'd wait for others to try new things first. Does five years leave room for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just about. If I wait a year for the others, I still get three or four years on the joysticks. That's enough to make the course worth it and to keep my pay up until I'm sixty-three. So yes, I'd still wait, just not very long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jonno, who's younger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to bet his life on the joysticks. He's thirty-four, he's got time to learn something the robots can't do yet, maybe fixing them. I'd tell him to use the five years like it's a warning bell. Funny, I'd give him braver advice than I'd take myself.

S3.say: Five years is enough for the government to set up retraining money and early pensions, and the union needs a plan now, not in year four. He'd even post about it.
S3.think: He'd get most of his working years in: a few years on the joysticks, then the robots take over about when he's ready to leave. It's bad for the young workers, not for him.
S3.do: Takes the tele-remote course around the second year once the first group is happy with it. Pays off the last of the loan on his work truck and helps the union rep list what each older worker would need.
S3.feel: Uneasy but able to see a path through, unlike the two-year picture.
S3.quote: Funny, I'd give him braver advice than I'd take myself.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is just enough room for his habit of letting others go first. He sees the timing as close to his planned retirement and turns his attention to younger crewmates. He noticed on his own that he'd give braver advice than he'd follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be retired before the robots really took over. That changes things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best chance we'll ever get to do it properly. Ten years is enough to build training, shorter work weeks, a share of the profits for the town. I'd say it at union meetings and at the bakery counter, people talk there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, it's almost nothing. I'll do my years, maybe learn the joysticks, and retire at sixty-three or sixty-four. What I think about is my daughter Lucia, she's a dental nurse, and whether her job is still around in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and saving like normal and take the tele-remote course when it makes sense. I'd keep going to union meetings and vote for whoever has an actual plan, not just speeches. I'd talk to Lucia about what she wants to do with the next ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for me. A bit of worry for Lucia, but nothing that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd start now, with ten years' warning, that you wouldn't bother with in the faster ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably take a proper course in something just for me, like bread-making with Ana. Sounds silly, but if robots are doing the work in 2036, I'd want something I like doing with my hands that isn't a job. With two years there's no space for that kind of thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still wait for others before learning the joysticks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh yes, even more so. With ten years there's no rush. I'd let the young blokes find all the bugs, and I'd go in when it's boring and works every time.

S4.say: This is the best chance to do it properly, with training, shorter weeks and a share of profits for the town. He'd say it at union meetings and the bakery counter.
S4.think: It barely affects him because he'll retire around sixty-three or sixty-four. He thinks more about whether his daughter's job as a dental nurse will last.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving and takes the tele-remote course when it makes sense. Goes to union meetings, votes for a party with a real plan and talks with his daughter about her next ten years.
S4.feel: Calm for himself, with a little worry for his daughter.
S4.quote: I'd want something I like doing with my hands that isn't a job.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade's warning Pedro relaxes completely and even starts thinking about life after work. His habit of letting others test new things first fits a slow timeline. His politics are consistent: fair sharing of the gains through unions and government.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Not for the end point, it's the same end point as the others, but because there's no time to learn anything and no time for the union to get organised. What would help is a proper redundancy package for older workers, a year's pay at least, and being able to draw my pension early without losing a chunk of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but robots underground could save lives, and nobody says that. I've seen a roof fall, I was lucky. If a machine can go in there instead of a man, part of me says good, just look after the man.

headlineQuote: Underground you look after each other, it's not a slogan, it's how you get home.
portrait: Pedro Olsen is a 58-year-old underground loader operator at a zinc mine, still junior after moving from thirty years of concrete work when his building firm folded. He is a union man at heart who wants any gains from automation shared through shorter shifts, training on paid time and fair redundancy, and he thinks about the weakest worker on his crew. He likes to let others test new technology first, which works well in the slower pictures, where he'd learn remote operation and ride out to retirement. Only the two-year AGI picture makes him anxious, because there's nothing left to learn into, though savings, a paid-off house and his wife's bakery keep him steady.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because there would be no time to learn anything new and no time for the union to get organised.
whatWouldHelp: A redundancy package of at least a year's pay for older workers, and being able to draw his pension early without losing a chunk of it.
